::: {.lead}
At 7.57 on a May morning in 2021, the Speaker's gavel finally fell on the
longest sitting of the decade. Parliament had argued about the EU recovery
package all night — and 99 % of the small-hours speeches came from a single
party. Interjections shouted across the chamber have doubled since 2015. The
word *polarisaatio* is uttered three times as often as a decade ago.

It certainly *feels* like Finnish politics is pulling apart. But feelings are
cheap. So we measured it: we taught a computer to guess which party a speaker
belongs to from a single plenary speech — no names, no party labels, just the
words — and watched how much easier that guess has become over three
parliamentary terms.
:::

## Parties have drifted apart — and the step came in 2023

Our headline measure is **separability**: how reliably two parties' speeches
can be told apart (0 = indistinguishable, 1 = always distinguishable).
Averaged over all 28 party pairs, it climbed from 0.39 to 0.45 to 0.56 across
the three terms. That is not a gentle drift. Most of the move happens in one
step.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-polarisation
#| fig-cap: "Mean separability over the 28 party pairs (0 = parties indistinguishable, 1 = always distinguishable). Bands: 10th–90th percentile over 8 repetitions. Random labels show the method finds no difference where none exists."
import pandas as pd
import plotly.graph_objects as go

s = pd.read_csv("../results/party_summary.csv")
fig = go.Figure()
for sarja, nimi, vari, leveys in [("real", "party labels", "#1f4e79", 4),
                                  ("random", "random labels", "#999999", 2.5)]:
    t = s[s["series"] == sarja].groupby("term")["polarisation"].agg(
        mean="mean", lo=lambda x: x.quantile(0.1), hi=lambda x: x.quantile(0.9))
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=t.index, y=t["mean"], mode="lines+markers", name=nimi,
        line={"color": vari, "width": leveys}, marker={"size": 12},
        error_y={"type": "data", "array": t["hi"] - t["mean"],
                 "arrayminus": t["mean"] - t["lo"], "thickness": 2}))
fig.add_annotation(x="2023-2027", y=0.56, text="the 2023 step", showarrow=True,
                   arrowhead=2, ax=-70, ay=10, font={"size": 13, "color": "#1f4e79"})
fig.update_layout(margin={"t": 60, "b": 10}, yaxis_title="separability",
                  xaxis_title=None, template="plotly_white", height=440,
                  font={"size": 14},
                  title={"text": "<b>One step, not a slow drift</b>",
                         "font": {"size": 19, "family": "Source Serif 4, Georgia, serif"}, "x": 0},
                  legend={"orientation": "h", "y": 1.02, "x": 0})
fig.show()
```

Why believe a computer's guessing game? Two checks. Shuffle the party labels
and repeat everything, and the measure collapses to zero — the method invents
nothing. And a completely different yardstick from the economics literature,
the leave-out estimator that @gentzkow2019 built for the US Congress and
@simola2023 applied to a century of Finnish parliamentary speech, ranks the
party pairs almost identically.

That second yardstick can be computed year by year, and it sharpens the
story: **flat from 2015 through 2022, rising from 2023 onwards.** What looks
like a decade-long trend is closer to a step change during the current term.
Part of the earlier rise even has a mundane explanation — speeches simply got
longer, and longer speeches are easier to classify. The jump after 2023
survives that correction.

## It is not just that parties talk about different things

An obvious objection: perhaps parties have not changed how they speak, only
what they speak about. The Finns Party talks about immigration, the Greens
about climate, and a word counter tells them apart without any polarisation
being involved.

So we repeated the measurement *inside* topics, using the topic keywords of a
recent study of Finnish social media [@gronow2024]. The objection fails.
Within every topic — climate, immigration, security, even the tax-heavy
inequality debate — parties have become easier to tell apart.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-topics
#| fig-cap: "Separability within the same topic (mean over the party pairs measurable in all three terms; topic keywords from @gronow2024). Inequality is mostly tax debate in parliament; COVID-19 spans only one term and is omitted."
KAUDET = ["2015-2019", "2019-2023", "2023-2027"]
VARIT = {"all speeches": "#2a78d6", "immigration": "#eb6834", "climate": "#1baf7a",
         "security": "#eda100", "inequality": "#e87ba4"}
NIMET = {"kaikki": "all speeches", "maahanmuutto": "immigration", "ilmasto": "climate",
         "turvallisuus": "security", "eriarvoisuus": "inequality"}

parit = pd.read_csv("../results/teemat_pairwise.csv")
parit = parit[(parit["malli"] == "party") & parit["teema"].isin(NIMET)]
fig = go.Figure()
for teema, nimi in NIMET.items():
    osa = parit[parit["teema"] == teema]
    kaikilla = osa.groupby(["a", "b"])["term"].nunique()
    parilista = kaikilla[kaikilla == 3].index
    osa = osa.set_index(["a", "b"]).loc[parilista].reset_index()
    sarja = osa.groupby("term")["d"].mean().reindex(KAUDET)
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=KAUDET, y=sarja, mode="lines+markers", name=nimi,
        line={"color": VARIT[nimi], "width": 3.5}, marker={"size": 11},
        hovertemplate=nimi + ", %{x}: %{y:.2f}<extra></extra>"))
    fig.add_annotation(x=KAUDET[-1], y=sarja.iloc[-1], text=nimi, showarrow=False,
                       xanchor="left", xshift=10,
                       font={"size": 12.5, "color": VARIT[nimi]})
fig.update_layout(template="plotly_white", showlegend=False, height=460,
                  margin={"t": 55, "b": 10, "l": 10, "r": 105},
                  font={"size": 14},
                  title={"text": "<b>Same topic, widening gap</b>",
                         "font": {"size": 19, "family": "Source Serif 4, Georgia, serif"}, "x": 0},
                  yaxis={"title": "separability", "rangemode": "tozero"},
                  xaxis={"title": None})
fig.show()
```

Parties are not merely choosing different subjects. They increasingly speak
about **the same subject in different ways**. The timing matches the Twitter
study, too: the gap between the Finns Party and the left-green parties on
climate doubled in 2019–23 — exactly when climate began to polarise on
Finnish social media. Part of the within-topic gap is institutional role,
since governments defend bills and oppositions attack them in the same
debate. Which is why the next finding matters.

## Two blocs

Which parties actually sound alike? The map below places parties so that the
ones our model confuses most often sit closest together. Press the buttons
and watch a decade of Finnish politics rearrange itself.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-map
#| fig-cap: "Party map: parties the model confuses most often sit closest together (classical multidimensional scaling on the separability matrix). Colours are the parties' official colours; pick the term with the buttons. Axes have no fixed meaning."
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "../src")
import config
from reporting import parimatriisi, klassinen_mds, kierra_kohti

parit = pd.read_csv("../results/party_pairwise.csv")
parit = parit[parit["series"] == "real"]

kartat, edellinen = {}, None
for kausi in KAUDET:
    xy = klassinen_mds(parimatriisi(parit[parit["term"] == kausi], "d").values)
    if edellinen is not None:
        xy = kierra_kohti(xy, edellinen)
    kartat[kausi] = xy
    edellinen = xy

fig = go.Figure()
for i, kausi in enumerate(KAUDET):
    xy = kartat[kausi]
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=xy[:, 0], y=xy[:, 1], mode="markers+text", visible=(i == 2),
        text=[config.PARTY_SHORT_EN[p] for p in config.MAIN_PARTIES],
        textposition="top center",
        textfont={"size": 14, "color": "#222"},
        marker={"size": 22, "color": [config.PARTY_COLORS[p] for p in config.MAIN_PARTIES],
                "line": {"width": 2.5, "color": "white"}},
        hovertemplate="%{text}<extra></extra>", showlegend=False))
fig.update_layout(
    template="plotly_white", height=500,
    margin={"t": 85, "b": 10, "l": 10, "r": 10}, font={"size": 14},
    title={"text": "<b>A decade rearranges itself</b>",
           "font": {"size": 19, "family": "Source Serif 4, Georgia, serif"}, "x": 0, "y": 0.97},
    xaxis={"visible": False}, yaxis={"visible": False, "scaleanchor": "x"},
    updatemenus=[{"type": "buttons", "direction": "right", "x": 0, "xanchor": "left",
                  "y": 1.10, "yanchor": "top",
                  "buttons": [{"label": kausi, "method": "update",
                               "args": [{"visible": [j == i for j in range(3)]}]}
                              for i, kausi in enumerate(KAUDET)],
                  "active": 2}])
fig.show()
```

Three things stand out.

**The right-side trio sounds alike everywhere.**
[NCP]{.party-chip style="background:#006288"}
[Finns]{.party-chip style="background:#C7A006"}
[CD]{.party-chip style="background:#8E6CC8"}
speak alike in every term — including 2019–23, when all three sat in
opposition. Their speech is more similar than their election-compass answers
would predict. Government status alone does not explain it: the five-party
Marin government spoke *less* cohesively than its three-party opposition.

**Close in views, far in voice.**
[Left]{.party-chip style="background:#F00A64"}
[SDP]{.party-chip style="background:#E11931"}
[Greens]{.party-chip style="background:#61BF1A"}
are among the closest pairs on the election compass, yet each speaks in its
own register.

**In 2023–27 the two dividing lines coincide for the first time.** The
right-side trio is now the core of the government, the left-green parties
lead the opposition, and the pairs across that line have become the most
separable pairs in parliament — 0.66 on average, against 0.45 two terms ago.
That coincidence is what produces the step in the first figure.

::: {.callout-note}
## How we measured this

We trained a classifier (TF-IDF features and logistic regression) to predict
the speaker's party from a single speech, separately for each term and eight
parties, from about 130,000 plenary speeches (2015 – Sep 2026, Parliament of
Finland open data). Names, party names and formulaic phrases are removed
before training. The model is always tested on **speakers it never saw during
training**, every party gets the same amount of training data, and every
number is reported against a shuffled-labels baseline — the precautions that
@gentzkow2019 show are necessary before reading classifier accuracy as
polarisation. Separability of a party pair is 2·AUC − 1 on the model's
probabilities; our cross-check is the leave-out estimator used by
@simola2023. Full details, robustness checks and code:
[the technical report and repository](https://github.com/jtompuri/data-science-mini-project).
:::

## Side notes from the transcripts

<!-- TODO (team decision pending): final selection of notebook 90 items. -->

The transcripts record more than words: every gavel knock, every burst of
laughter, every interjection. A few favourites from the margins of the data:

**Parliament heckles along bloc lines.** Interjections have doubled — from
about 28 per hundred speeches in 2015–19 to 56 now — and their direction
follows the blocs: left-green MPs heckle the National Coalition and the Finns
Party, and vice versa.

**The chamber has noticed its own drift.** The stem *polaris-* appears three
times as often in the current term (22 occurrences per million words) as in
2015–19 — and the number of different MPs using it has grown at the same
rate.

**Every year has its word.** The fastest-rising stems trace the decade:

::: {.year-strip}
[**2016** kiky]{.chip}
[**2017** aktiivimalli]{.chip}
[**2018** osakesäästötili]{.chip}
[**2019** terapiatakuu]{.chip}
[**2020** korona]{.chip}
[**2021** koronapassi]{.chip}
[**2022** Ukraina]{.chip}
[**2023** indeksijäädytys]{.chip}
[**2024** sovittelija]{.chip}
[**2025** velkajarru]{.chip}
:::

**And the longest night** belongs to the EU recovery package: the sitting of
12 May 2021 ended at 7.57 the next morning, and 99 % of the small-hours
speeches came from one party — the Finns Party.

## What this does and does not show

Three caveats belong in any honest reading. First, three terms means three
different governments: with these data, a time trend cannot be fully
separated from who happens to govern. Second, we measure **language, not
opinions** — though the speech distances do match election-compass distances
in the two most recent terms. Third, the smallest parties (the Christian
Democrats and the Swedish People's Party) have so few MPs that their numbers
are noisy, and the current term is still incomplete (data to September 2026).
Unlike @simola2023, we do not control for MPs' region or gender.

What the data do show is specific: a measurable, robust widening of the
linguistic distance between Finnish parties, concentrated in the current
term, visible within topics, and organised around two blocs whose boundary
now coincides with the government–opposition divide.
